rd-school-c12-chemistry-b.ch06-haloalkan.title: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes (part 2)
rd-school-c12-chemistry-b.ch06-haloalkan.subtitle: Chirality, reactivity orders, haloarene inertness and named reactions

sections.h: Optical activity and chirality in depth
sections.md:
Plane-polarised light is rotated by some compounds. A compound rotating it clockwise is **dextrorotatory (d or +)**; anticlockwise, **laevorotatory (l or −)**. Rotation is measured with a **polarimeter**.

A carbon bearing four different groups is **asymmetric (chiral)**. The molecule and its mirror image are non-superimposable: they are **enantiomers**, with identical physical properties except the direction of rotation. Butan-2-ol is chiral; propan-2-ol is not, because its central carbon has two CH₃ groups.

A 50:50 mixture of enantiomers is a **racemic mixture** (dl or ±) with zero rotation; making one is **racemisation**.

**Retention** keeps the spatial arrangement at the chiral centre; **inversion** flips it like an umbrella in the wind.
- SN2: complete inversion (backside attack).
- SN1: through a planar carbocation, attack from both faces → racemisation (mostly).

check.q: Which compound is chiral?
check.why: C-2 of 2-chlorobutane carries H, Cl, CH₃ and C₂H₅ — four different groups.

sections.md:
- **SN2** (steric hindrance controls): CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°.
- **SN1** (carbocation stability controls): 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X. Allylic and benzylic halides are very reactive by SN1 because their carbocations are resonance-stabilised.
- For the same alkyl group, leaving-group ability: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F.
- Polar protic solvents favour SN1.

**Ambident nucleophiles**: KCN (ionic) gives mainly alkyl cyanides because C is attacked through carbon, whereas AgCN (covalent) gives isocyanides. KNO₂ gives alkyl nitrites (R–O–N=O); AgNO₂ gives nitroalkanes (R–NO₂).

**Elimination (Saytzeff/Zaitsev rule)**: in dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic KOH, the more substituted alkene is the major product. 2-bromobutane gives but-2-ene (81%) over but-1-ene. Strong bulky bases and high temperature favour elimination; weak bases and aqueous medium favour substitution.

check.q: Reaction of R–Br with AgCN mainly gives:
check.why: AgCN is largely covalent, so the nitrogen lone pair attacks, giving isocyanide R–NC.

sections.md:
Chlorobenzene does not react with NaOH under ordinary conditions. Reasons:
1. **Resonance** — the lone pair on Cl delocalises into the ring, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character; it is shorter and stronger.
2. **sp² carbon** — more s-character, holds the electron pair more tightly.
3. **Instability of the phenyl cation** — rules out SN1.
4. **Repulsion** — the electron-rich ring repels an approaching nucleophile; backside attack is blocked.

Under harsh conditions (Dow process: NaOH, 623 K, 300 atm) chlorobenzene gives phenol. **Electron-withdrawing groups (–NO₂) at ortho and para positions** make substitution easier: 4-nitrochlorobenzene reacts at 443 K, and 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene merely with warm water.

In **electrophilic substitution**, halogen is deactivating (–I effect) yet **ortho/para directing** (+R effect): halogenation, nitration, sulphonation and Friedel–Crafts reactions give mainly the para isomer.

sections.h: Named reactions: Wurtz, Wurtz–Fittig, Fittig, Finkelstein, Swarts, Sandmeyer
sections.md:
| Reaction | Reagents | Product |
|---|---|---|
| Wurtz | 2 R–X + 2Na, dry ether | R–R |
| Wurtz–Fittig | Ar–X + R–X + Na, dry ether | Ar–R (alkylbenzene) |
| Fittig | 2 Ar–X + Na, dry ether | Ar–Ar (biphenyl) |
| Finkelstein | R–Cl/R–Br + NaI in dry acetone | R–I (NaCl/NaBr precipitates) |
| Swarts | R–Br/R–Cl + AgF, Hg₂F₂, CoF₂ or SbF₃ | R–F |
| Sandmeyer | ArN₂⁺ + CuCl/HCl or CuBr/HBr | Ar–Cl / Ar–Br |

**Grignard reagent**: R–X + Mg in dry ether → RMgX. It is very reactive with any proton source (water, alcohols, amines) giving hydrocarbons, so it must be kept dry: RMgX + H₂O → RH + Mg(OH)X.

check.why: In the Fittig reaction two aryl halides couple with sodium in dry ether to give a diaryl.

sections.h: Polyhalogen compounds — uses and environmental effects
sections.md:
- **Dichloromethane**: paint remover, solvent; may harm the nervous system, skin and eyes.
- **Chloroform**: solvent; was an anaesthetic; slowly oxidised by air and light to poisonous **phosgene** (COCl₂), so stored in dark coloured, filled bottles.
- **Iodoform**: once an antiseptic because it releases free iodine; replaced due to its smell.
- **Carbon tetrachloride**: refrigerants and propellants formerly; damages the liver, depletes ozone.
- **Freons (CFCs)**: refrigeration and aerosols; in the stratosphere UV breaks them into chlorine radicals that destroy ozone.
- **DDT**: first chlorinated insecticide, effective against malaria and typhus vectors; but it is not metabolised quickly, accumulates in fatty tissue up the food chain, and insects developed resistance — banned in many countries (India restricts it to limited public-health use).

rd-school-c12-chemistry-b.ch07-alcohols-.title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
rd-school-c12-chemistry-b.ch07-alcohols-.subtitle: Sanitiser, Dettol-like antiseptics and anaesthetic ether — the many lives of the –OH group

sections.md:
The hand sanitiser at your school gate is mostly ethanol or isopropyl alcohol. The sugar in your chai has many –OH groups; so does the cotton of your shirt (cellulose). Phenol derivatives are found in antiseptics; ether was among the first anaesthetics.

- **Alcohols**: –OH attached to an sp³ carbon of an alkyl group (R–OH).
- **Phenols**: –OH attached directly to an aromatic ring carbon (Ar–OH).
- **Ethers**: an oxygen joined to two alkyl/aryl groups (R–O–R′); formally, H of –OH replaced by R.

**Classification of alcohols and phenols**
- By number of –OH: **monohydric**, **dihydric** (ethane-1,2-diol, glycol), **trihydric** (propane-1,2,3-triol, glycerol); phenols similarly (catechol is dihydric).
- Monohydric alcohols with **C(sp³)–OH**: primary (1°), secondary (2°), tertiary (3°) depending on the carbon bearing –OH; **allylic** alcohols (–OH next to C=C) and **benzylic** alcohols (–OH next to ring), each also 1°/2°/3°.
- **C(sp²)–OH**: **vinylic** alcohols (CH₂=CH–OH, unstable) and **phenols**.

**Classification of ethers**: **simple/symmetrical** (both groups same, C₂H₅OC₂H₅) or **mixed/unsymmetrical** (CH₃OC₂H₅, C₆H₅OCH₃).

check.q: C₆H₅CH₂OH is a
check.why: The –OH is on an sp³ CH₂ carbon attached to a benzene ring, which makes it a 1° benzylic alcohol.

sections.h: 2. Nomenclature and structure of functional groups
sections.md:
**Alcohols**: common name = alkyl + alcohol (methyl alcohol, isopropyl alcohol). IUPAC: replace -e of alkane by **-ol**, number chain from end nearer –OH: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ propan-2-ol; (CH₃)₃COH 2-methylpropan-2-ol; HOCH₂CH₂OH ethane-1,2-diol; glycerol propane-1,2,3-triol. Cyclic: cyclohexanol.

**Phenols**: the simplest hydroxy benzene is **phenol** (also IUPAC). Cresols are methylphenols (o-cresol = 2-methylphenol). Dihydroxybenzenes: benzene-1,2-diol (catechol), benzene-1,3-diol (resorcinol), benzene-1,4-diol (hydroquinone/quinol).

**Ethers**: common names list alkyl groups alphabetically + ether (ethyl methyl ether; diethyl ether). IUPAC: **alkoxyalkane** — the larger group is the parent: CH₃OCH₂CH₃ methoxyethane; C₆H₅OCH₃ methoxybenzene (anisole); C₆H₅OC₂H₅ ethoxybenzene (phenetole).

**Structures**:
- In alcohols the O is sp³; C–O–H angle ≈ 108.9° (slightly less than tetrahedral, due to lone-pair repulsion).
- In phenol the C–O bond (136 pm) is shorter than in methanol (142 pm) because (i) the O lone pair is partly conjugated with the ring, giving partial double-bond character, and (ii) the carbon is sp².
- In ethers the C–O–C angle (≈111.7° in methoxymethane) is slightly larger than tetrahedral because of repulsion between bulky alkyl groups; C–O bond ≈ 141 pm.

check.q: The IUPAC name of C₆H₅OCH₃ is
check.why: Ethers are named alkoxyalkanes/arenes; the methoxy group sits on the benzene parent.

sections.md:
**1. From alkenes**
- *Acid-catalysed hydration*: alkene + H₂O (H⁺) → alcohol, following Markovnikov's rule. Mechanism: (i) protonation of alkene to a carbocation; (ii) water attacks the carbocation; (iii) deprotonation. E.g. CH₃CH=CH₂ → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃.
- *Hydroboration–oxidation* (H.C. Brown, Nobel 1979): diborane (BH₃)₂ adds to the alkene giving trialkyl borane, then H₂O₂/NaOH oxidises it. Net result is **anti-Markovnikov** addition of water: propene → propan-1-ol, in excellent yield.

**2. From carbonyl compounds**
- *Reduction of aldehydes and ketones*: H₂ with Pt/Pd/Ni, or NaBH₄ / LiAlH₄. Aldehydes → 1° alcohols; ketones → 2° alcohols.
- *Reduction of carboxylic acids and esters*: LiAlH₄ reduces acids to 1° alcohols (expensive; in industry acids are first esterified and the ester is hydrogenated catalytically).

**3. From Grignard reagents** — RMgX adds to the C=O carbon, and hydrolysis of the adduct gives the alcohol:
- with methanal (HCHO) → **1° alcohol**
- with other aldehydes → **2° alcohol**
- with ketones → **3° alcohol**

E.g. CH₃MgBr + CH₃COCH₃ → then H₂O → (CH₃)₃COH.

sections.md:
Phenol (carbolic acid) was first isolated from coal tar in the early 19th century. Today most is made synthetically.

1. **From haloarenes**: chlorobenzene + NaOH at 623 K, 320 atm → sodium phenoxide; acidify → phenol.
2. **From benzenesulphonic acid**: benzene + oleum → benzenesulphonic acid; fuse with molten NaOH → sodium phenoxide; acidify → phenol.
3. **From diazonium salts**: aniline + HNO₂ (NaNO₂ + HCl) at 273–278 K → benzenediazonium chloride; warm with water (or treat with dilute acid) → phenol + N₂ + HCl.
4. **From cumene** (industrial, most phenol worldwide): benzene + propene → cumene (isopropylbenzene); air oxidation → cumene hydroperoxide; dilute acid → phenol + **acetone** (a valuable by-product).

check.q: The cumene process gives phenol and
check.why: Acid treatment of cumene hydroperoxide splits it into phenol and propanone (acetone).

sections.h: 5. Physical properties of alcohols and phenols
sections.md:
The –OH group has a polar O–H bond, giving **hydrogen bonding**.

**Boiling points** rise with the number of carbons (stronger van der Waals forces) and fall with branching. Alcohols and phenols boil much higher than hydrocarbons, ethers and haloalkanes of similar mass: ethanol (46 g/mol) boils at 351 K, methoxymethane (46) at 248 K, propane (44) at 231 K. The reason is **intermolecular hydrogen bonding** between –OH groups, absent in ethers and hydrocarbons.

**Solubility** in water: lower alcohols are fully miscible because they form hydrogen bonds with water. Solubility falls as the hydrophobic alkyl part grows (butanol is only partly soluble, hexanol barely). Phenol is moderately soluble.

check.q: Ethanol boils far higher than methoxymethane though both have M = 46 because
check.why: Ethanol molecules are linked by O–H···O hydrogen bonds, which need extra energy to break.

sections.md:
Alcohols react as **nucleophiles** (O lone pair attacks electrophiles) and, when protonated, as **electrophiles** (C–O breaks). Reactions break either O–H or C–O.

**(a) Acidity of alcohols** — reaction with active metals: 2R–OH + 2Na → 2R–ONa (sodium alkoxide) + H₂. Phenols also react with Na and with **aqueous NaOH** (alcohols do not).

Alcohols are weaker acids than water. Electron-releasing alkyl groups increase electron density on O, destabilising the alkoxide; acidity order: **1° > 2° > 3°**. Alkoxide ions are stronger bases than OH⁻: RO⁻ + H₂O → ROH + OH⁻. Alcohols also act as Brønsted bases (accepting H⁺ on oxygen).

**(b) Acidity of phenols** — phenol (pKa ≈ 10.0) is far more acidic than ethanol (pKa ≈ 15.9). The –OH on an sp² carbon is more polar, and the **phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised** (negative charge delocalised over the ring), more than phenol itself (whose resonance involves charge separation).
- **Electron-withdrawing groups** (–NO₂) at o/p increase acidity: p-nitrophenol (7.1), 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid, 0.5) is a strong acid.
- **Electron-releasing groups** (–CH₃, alkyl) decrease acidity: cresols are weaker acids than phenol.

**(c) Esterification**: alcohols and phenols + carboxylic acids (conc. H₂SO₄, reversible; remove water to push forward), acid chlorides or anhydrides (with pyridine to neutralise HCl) → esters. Acetylation of salicylic acid gives **aspirin** (acetylsalicylic acid), a painkiller and anti-inflammatory.

sections.md:
**(a) With hydrogen halides**: ROH + HX → RX + H₂O. **Lucas test** (conc. HCl + ZnCl₂, the Lucas reagent) distinguishes classes: **3° alcohols turn turbid immediately**, 2° in about five minutes, 1° do not at room temperature (they need heating). Turbidity = insoluble alkyl chloride.

**(b) With phosphorus trihalides**: 3ROH + PBr₃ → 3RBr + H₃PO₃.

**(c) Dehydration** with protic acids (conc. H₂SO₄, H₃PO₄) or ZnCl₂/alumina → alkenes:
- Ethanol: conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K → ethene.
- 2° alcohols: 85% H₃PO₄ at 440 K; 3° alcohols: 20% H₃PO₄ at 358 K.
- Ease: **3° > 2° > 1°**. Mechanism: (i) protonation of –OH; (ii) slow loss of water → carbocation; (iii) loss of β-H⁺ → alkene.

**(d) Oxidation** (loss of H from O and C):
- 1° alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid with strong oxidants (acidified KMnO₄). To stop at the aldehyde use **PCC** (pyridinium chlorochromate, CrO₃·C₅H₅N·HCl) or CrO₃ in anhydrous medium.
- 2° alcohol → ketone (CrO₃).
- 3° alcohols resist oxidation; strong agents at high temperature break C–C bonds to give mixtures of acids with fewer carbons.
- Vapours over **heated copper at 573 K** dehydrogenate: 1° → aldehyde, 2° → ketone, 3° → alkene (dehydration).

> Biological note: in the body, methanol is oxidised to methanal then methanoic acid, which can cause blindness and death — that is why spurious liquor kills. Ethanol is treated as an antidote in hospitals.

check.q: With Lucas reagent, immediate turbidity indicates a
check.why: Tertiary alcohols form stable carbocations fastest, so the insoluble alkyl chloride appears immediately.

sections.md:
**Electrophilic aromatic substitution**: –OH is strongly **activating and ortho/para-directing** (resonance raises electron density at o/p).
- **Nitration**: dilute HNO₃ at 298 K → o- and p-nitrophenol, separable by **steam distillation**: o-nitrophenol is steam-volatile (intramolecular H-bond), p-nitrophenol is not (intermolecular H-bonding). Conc. HNO₃ → **2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid)**; yield is poor, so in practice phenol is first sulphonated then nitrated.
- **Halogenation**: Br₂ in a low-polarity solvent (CHCl₃, CS₂) at low temperature → mono-bromophenols (mainly para). **Bromine water** → white precipitate of **2,4,6-tribromophenol** at once (phenol polarises Br₂ even without Lewis acid).

**Kolbe's reaction**: sodium phenoxide + CO₂ (then H⁺) → **salicylic acid** (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) — phenoxide is even more reactive than phenol toward the weak electrophile CO₂.

**Reimer–Tiemann reaction**: phenol + CHCl₃ + aqueous NaOH → substituted benzal chloride intermediate → hydrolysed to **salicylaldehyde** (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde) on acidification.

**With zinc dust**: phenol → benzene.

**Oxidation**: with chromic acid → **benzoquinone** (a conjugated diketone); phenols left in air slowly turn dark (quinones form).

check.q: Phenol with bromine water gives
check.why: –OH strongly activates all ortho and para positions, so three bromine atoms enter instantly forming a white precipitate.

sections.md:
**Methanol (wood spirit)** was once made by destructive distillation of wood. Now: CO + 2H₂ → CH₃OH over ZnO–Cr₂O₃ at 573–673 K and 200–300 atm. Colourless, b.p. 337 K, **highly poisonous** — small quantities cause blindness, larger ones death. Used as a solvent in paints and varnishes and to make formaldehyde.

**Ethanol** is made by **fermentation** of sugars, e.g. molasses (sugarcane by-product — India is a major producer), fruits like grapes. Enzyme **invertase** converts sucrose to glucose and fructose; **zymase** (from yeast) converts these to ethanol and CO₂. Air must be kept out, or ethanol oxidises to ethanoic acid (vinegar taste). Ethanol is a colourless liquid, b.p. 351 K, used as solvent in paint, in making carbon compounds and as fuel. Industrial ethanol is made unfit for drinking by adding copper sulphate (colour) and pyridine (foul smell) — **denaturation**. India's ethanol blending programme mixes it with petrol (E20 fuel).

check.q: Denaturation of alcohol means
options: making it unfit for drinking by adding CuSO₄ and pyridine
check.why: Adding colouring and foul-smelling substances prevents misuse of tax-cheaper industrial alcohol.

sections.md:
**Preparation**
1. **Dehydration of alcohols**: excess ethanol with conc. H₂SO₄ at 413 K → ethoxyethane (at 443 K, ethene forms instead). Mechanism: protonated alcohol is attacked (SN2) by another alcohol molecule. Suitable only for symmetrical ethers from 1° alcohols; 2° and 3° alcohols give alkenes.
2. **Williamson synthesis** (both symmetrical and unsymmetrical): R–X + R′–O⁻Na⁺ → R–O–R′ + NaX. It is SN2, so the halide should be **primary**; with tertiary halides elimination dominates. To make (CH₃)₃C–O–CH₃, use CH₃Br + (CH₃)₃CONa, not (CH₃)₃CBr + CH₃ONa. Phenols give aryl ethers: C₆H₅ONa + CH₃I → anisole.

**Physical properties**: C–O bonds are polar (net dipole). Boiling points resemble alkanes of similar mass and are much lower than alcohols (no hydrogen bonding between molecules). Miscibility in water resembles alcohols of similar mass (ether oxygen accepts H-bonds from water): methoxyethane and butan-1-ol are similarly soluble.

**Chemical reactions**
- **Cleavage by HX**: R–O–R + HX → RX + ROH (excess HX gives two RX). Reactivity HI > HBr > HCl. With a primary + tertiary group, the halide forms on the tertiary carbon (SN1 via stable carbocation); for methyl + 1°/2° alkyl, iodide goes to the methyl (SN2 at less hindered carbon). Alkyl aryl ethers give **phenol + alkyl halide** (Ar–O bond has partial double bond character and phenyl cation is unstable): anisole + HI → phenol + CH₃I.
- **Electrophilic substitution** of aromatic ethers: –OR is o,p-directing and activating.
  - Bromination: anisole + Br₂ in ethanoic acid (no catalyst) → mainly p-bromoanisole.
  - Friedel–Crafts: with CH₃Cl/AlCl₃ → 2- and 4-methoxytoluene; with CH₃COCl/AlCl₃ → 2- and 4-methoxyacetophenone.
  - Nitration: conc. H₂SO₄/HNO₃ → 2- and 4-nitroanisole.

Uses: diethyl ether is a common solvent and was historically an anaesthetic.

rd-school-c12-chemistry-b.ch07-alcohols-.title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers (part 2)
rd-school-c12-chemistry-b.ch07-alcohols-.subtitle: Distinction tests, named reactions of phenol, mechanisms and ether cleavage

sections.md:
Phenol (pKa ≈ 10) is far more acidic than ethanol (pKa ≈ 15.9) because the phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance — the negative charge spreads over the ring's ortho and para carbons.

- **Electron-withdrawing groups** (–NO₂) at ortho/para increase acidity: o-nitrophenol pKa 7.2, p-nitrophenol 7.1, and 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (**picric acid**) pKa 0.71 — almost as strong as a mineral acid. m-nitrophenol (8.3) is helped only by the inductive effect.
- **Electron-releasing groups** (–CH₃) decrease acidity: cresols have pKa about 10.2.

In alcohols, acidity falls 1° > 2° > 3° because alkyl groups push electron density toward oxygen. Alcohols react with Na metal (2ROH + 2Na → 2RONa + H₂) but not with NaOH; phenol reacts with both, yet not with NaHCO₃ (it is weaker than carbonic acid).

check.q: Which is the most acidic?
check.why: The –NO₂ group at the para position withdraws electrons by resonance and induction, stabilising the phenoxide ion most.

sections.md:
Ethanol with conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K gives ethene in three steps:
1. **Protonation**: C₂H₅OH + H⁺ → C₂H₅OH₂⁺ (fast).
2. **Carbocation formation**: loss of water gives CH₃CH₂⁺ (slow, rate-determining).
3. **Loss of a proton** from the β-carbon gives CH₂=CH₂.

Ease of dehydration: 3° > 2° > 1°, following carbocation stability. Tertiary alcohols dehydrate with 20% H₃PO₄ at 358 K; primary need conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K.

At **413 K with excess ethanol**, the protonated alcohol is attacked by another ethanol (SN2) giving **diethyl ether** — the same reagent makes either product depending on temperature.

**Mechanism of hydration of alkenes** is the reverse: protonation of the alkene → carbocation → water attacks → deprotonation; Markovnikov orientation results.

**Lucas reagent** (conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl₂) converts alcohols to chlorides, which are insoluble and make the solution turbid:
- 3° — turbidity **immediately**
- 2° — within about **five minutes**
- 1° — **no turbidity** at room temperature (only on heating)

**Oxidation and dehydrogenation**: over heated copper at 573 K, 1° alcohols give aldehydes, 2° give ketones, 3° undergo dehydration to alkenes.

**Phenol vs alcohol**: phenol gives a violet colour with neutral FeCl₃ solution and a white precipitate with bromine water; alcohols do neither.

check.q: An alcohol gives immediate turbidity with Lucas reagent. It is:
check.why: 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary; its stable carbocation forms the chloride at once.

sections.md:
- **Nitration**: dilute HNO₃ at 298 K gives o- and p-nitrophenol; separated by **steam distillation** because o-nitrophenol has intramolecular hydrogen bonding (volatile), while p-nitrophenol has intermolecular H-bonding. Conc. HNO₃ gives picric acid.
- **Bromination**: in CS₂ at low temperature → mono-bromophenols; with bromine water → white precipitate of **2,4,6-tribromophenol**. The –OH group activates the ring so strongly that the Lewis acid is not needed.
- **Kolbe's reaction**: sodium phenoxide + CO₂ (4–7 atm, 400 K), then acid → **salicylic acid** (2-hydroxybenzoic acid), which with acetic anhydride gives aspirin.
- **Reimer–Tiemann reaction**: phenol + CHCl₃ + aqueous NaOH, then acid → **salicylaldehyde**; the intermediate is a substituted benzal chloride.
- **Reaction with zinc dust**: phenol → benzene.
- **Oxidation**: with chromic acid → **benzoquinone**; on standing in air phenol slowly darkens forming quinones.

check.q: Kolbe's reaction gives:
check.why: Phenoxide ion, a strong nucleophile, attacks weakly electrophilic CO₂ at the ortho position; acidification gives salicylic acid.

sections.h: Ethers: Williamson's synthesis limits and cleavage by HX
sections.md:
**Williamson synthesis**: R–X + R′–ONa → R–O–R′ + NaX (SN2). Use a **primary** alkyl halide and the bulkier alkoxide. A tertiary halide with alkoxide gives an **alkene** by elimination instead, so (CH₃)₃C–O–CH₃ is made from (CH₃)₃CONa + CH₃Br, not from (CH₃)₃CBr + CH₃ONa.

**Cleavage with HI** (reactivity HI > HBr > HCl):
- Two primary/methyl groups: the halide attacks the smaller group (SN2), giving CH₃I + ROH.
- One tertiary group: SN1, the halide ends on the tertiary carbon: (CH₃)₃C–O–CH₃ + HI → (CH₃)₃C–I + CH₃OH.
- **Alkyl aryl ethers** always give **phenol + alkyl halide**, because the O–aryl bond has partial double-bond character and phenyl cations do not form: C₆H₅OCH₃ + HI → C₆H₅OH + CH₃I.

**Electrophilic substitution in anisole**: –OCH₃ is o/p-directing and activating. Bromination (Br₂ in ethanoic acid, no catalyst) → mainly p-bromoanisole; Friedel–Crafts alkylation/acylation and nitration give o- and p-products, para major.

**Physical properties**: ethers have dipole moments but no O–H, so boiling points are close to alkanes of similar mass and much lower than alcohols; their solubility in water resembles alcohols because they accept hydrogen bonds.

workedExamples.q: Give the products of 1-methoxy-2-methylpropane... rather, of methoxybenzene with HI.
steps: Aryl–O bond is strong (partial double bond)

workedExamples.q: How is propan-2-ol distinguished from 2-methylpropan-2-ol?
workedExamples.answer: By the Lucas test (time to turbidity)

summary: Phenoxide resonance makes phenol more acidic than alcohols
–NO₂ at o/p increases acidity; –CH₃ decreases it
Alcohol acidity: 1° > 2° > 3°
Dehydration: protonation → carbocation (slow) → alkene; 3° easiest
443 K → ethene; 413 K → diethyl ether
Lucas test: 3° immediate, 2° ~5 min, 1° none
Phenol: violet with FeCl₃, white ppt with bromine water
o-/p-nitrophenol separated by steam distillation
Kolbe → salicylic acid; Reimer–Tiemann → salicylaldehyde
Williamson needs a primary halide
Anisole + HI → phenol + CH₃I

rd-school-c12-chemistry-b.ch08-aldehydes.title: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
rd-school-c12-chemistry-b.ch08-aldehydes.subtitle: The smell of cinnamon, the sourness of vinegar and the nail-polish remover — all from the carbonyl group

sections.h: 1. The carbonyl group and its family
sections.md:
Open a jar of dalchini (cinnamon) — that warm smell is cinnamaldehyde. Vanilla in ice cream is vanillin, another aldehyde. Nail-polish remover is acetone, a ketone. The sourness of vinegar comes from ethanoic acid, a carboxylic acid. All contain the **carbonyl group, >C=O**.

- **Aldehydes**: carbonyl bonded to at least one H (R–CHO).
- **Ketones**: carbonyl bonded to two carbon groups (R–CO–R′).
- **Carboxylic acids**: carbonyl bonded to –OH (R–COOH), the **carboxyl** group.
- **Acid derivatives**: amides (–CONH₂), acyl halides (–COX), esters (–COOR′), anhydrides (–CO–O–CO–).

They are used as solvents, flavourings, perfumes, medicines, plastics and fabrics (polyester). Formalin (40% methanal) preserves biological specimens.

check.q: Acetone (CH₃COCH₃) is a
check.why: Its carbonyl carbon is attached to two methyl groups, the defining feature of a ketone.

sections.h: 2. Nomenclature and structure of the carbonyl group
sections.md:
**Common names**: aldehydes from the corresponding acid: formaldehyde (HCHO), acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO), benzaldehyde. Positions on the chain use Greek letters α, β, γ from the carbon next to CHO. Ketones: alkyl groups alphabetically + ketone (ethyl methyl ketone); dimethyl ketone = acetone; C₆H₅COCH₃ = acetophenone, C₆H₅COC₆H₅ = benzophenone.

**IUPAC**: aldehydes: -e of alkane → **-al** (ethanal, propanal; CHO carbon is C-1). Ketones: → **-one**, with position number (butan-2-one, pentan-3-one). For rings with –CHO attached: *carbaldehyde* (cyclohexanecarbaldehyde); benzaldehyde = benzenecarbaldehyde.

**Structure**: the carbonyl carbon is **sp²**, forming three σ bonds in a plane (≈120°) and one π bond with oxygen. Oxygen is more electronegative, so the C=O bond is **polar** — carbon is a Lewis acid (electrophilic) and oxygen a Lewis base (nucleophilic). Resonance (C=O ↔ C⁺–O⁻) explains the high dipole moment (2.3–2.8 D) and reactivity toward nucleophiles.

check.q: The carbonyl carbon is
check.why: It is sp² hybridised and carries a partial positive charge because oxygen pulls electron density.

sections.md:
**General methods**
1. **Oxidation of alcohols**: 1° → aldehydes (PCC, or K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺ removing aldehyde as it forms); 2° → ketones.
2. **Dehydrogenation**: alcohol vapour over Ag or Cu at 573 K — best for volatile alcohols, industrially important.
3. **Ozonolysis of alkenes**: O₃ then Zn/H₂O cleaves C=C → aldehydes/ketones depending on substitution.
4. **Hydration of alkynes**: ethyne + H₂O (H₂SO₄ + HgSO₄) → ethanal; other alkynes → ketones.

**Aldehydes only**
1. **From acyl chlorides — Rosenmund reduction**: RCOCl + H₂ over Pd on BaSO₄ (poisoned so it stops at aldehyde) → RCHO.
2. **From nitriles and esters — Stephen reaction**: RCN + SnCl₂/HCl → imine → hydrolysis → RCHO. DIBAL-H (diisobutylaluminium hydride) also reduces nitriles and esters to aldehydes.
3. **From hydrocarbons (aromatic aldehydes)**:
   - *Etard reaction*: toluene + chromyl chloride (CrO₂Cl₂) in CS₂ → chromium complex → benzaldehyde.
   - With CrO₃ in acetic anhydride → benzylidene diacetate → hydrolysis → benzaldehyde.
   - Side-chain chlorination of toluene → benzal chloride → hydrolysis at 373 K → benzaldehyde (industrial).
   - **Gatterman–Koch**: benzene + CO + HCl (anhydrous AlCl₃/CuCl) → benzaldehyde.

**Ketones only**
1. **From acyl chlorides** with dialkylcadmium: 2RCOCl + R′₂Cd → 2RCOR′ + CdCl₂.
2. **From nitriles** with Grignard reagent, then hydrolysis: CH₃CH₂CN + C₆H₅MgBr → propiophenone.
3. **Friedel–Crafts acylation**: benzene + RCOCl / AlCl₃ → C₆H₅COR.

check.q: Rosenmund reduction converts
check.why: Hydrogen over poisoned Pd/BaSO₄ reduces an acid chloride only as far as the aldehyde.

sections.md:
Methanal is a gas; ethanal is volatile (b.p. 294 K); other aldehydes and ketones are liquids or solids.

**Boiling points** are higher than hydrocarbons and ethers of similar mass (dipole–dipole attractions) but lower than alcohols (no intermolecular hydrogen bonding). For mass ≈ 58: butane 273 K, methoxyethane 281 K, propanal 322 K, acetone 329 K, propan-1-ol 370 K.

**Solubility**: lower members (methanal, ethanal, propanone) are miscible with water — they form hydrogen bonds with water; solubility falls rapidly as the alkyl chain lengthens. All dissolve in organic solvents.

**Smell**: lower aldehydes have sharp, pungent odours; as size grows, odours become fragrant. Many natural fragrances are aldehydes and ketones.

check.q: Propanal boils lower than propan-1-ol because
options: it cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds
check.why: Aldehydes have no O–H, so they lack the strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding that alcohols have.

sections.h: 5. Reactions of aldehydes and ketones: nucleophilic addition
sections.md:
**Mechanism**: a nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon perpendicular to the plane of sp² orbitals; carbon becomes sp³ and a **tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate** forms; it picks up a proton to give the neutral product.

**Reactivity**: **aldehydes > ketones**, for two reasons — *steric*: two bulky groups on ketones hinder approach; *electronic*: two alkyl groups release electrons and reduce the δ+ on carbon. Benzaldehyde is less reactive than propanal because the ring's resonance reduces electrophilicity.

**Important additions**
1. **HCN** → **cyanohydrins** (base-catalysed; CN⁻ is the real nucleophile). Useful synthetic intermediates.
2. **Sodium hydrogensulphite (NaHSO₃)** → crystalline bisulphite addition compounds; reversible with dilute acid or alkali — used to **separate and purify** aldehydes.
3. **Grignard reagents** → alcohols (see previous chapter).
4. **Alcohols**: aldehydes + one equivalent monohydric alcohol (dry HCl) → **hemiacetal**; + another → **acetal** (gem-dialkoxy). Ketones + ethylene glycol → cyclic **ketal**. Acetals hydrolyse back with aqueous acid — used to **protect** carbonyl groups.
5. **Ammonia derivatives (H₂N–Z)** — addition then loss of water (addition–elimination), pH-dependent:

| Reagent | Product |
|---|---|
| NH₂OH (hydroxylamine) | oxime |
| NH₂NH₂ (hydrazine) | hydrazone |
| C₆H₅NHNH₂ | phenylhydrazone |
| 2,4-DNP (Brady's reagent) | 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone (yellow-orange-red ppt; test for carbonyl) |
| NH₂NHCONH₂ | semicarbazone |

check.q: Which is most reactive toward nucleophilic addition?
check.why: Methanal has no alkyl groups, so it is the least hindered and its carbon is the most electrophilic.

sections.md:
**Reduction**
- To alcohols: NaBH₄, LiAlH₄ or catalytic H₂: aldehydes → 1°, ketones → 2° alcohols.
- To hydrocarbons (C=O → CH₂): **Clemmensen reduction** (Zn–Hg + conc. HCl) or **Wolff–Kishner reduction** (NH₂NH₂, then KOH in ethylene glycol on heating).

**Oxidation** — aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids (even by mild agents); ketones need strong oxidants and harsh conditions, breaking C–C bonds (Popoff's rule broadly: the carbonyl stays with the smaller group).
- **Tollens' test**: ammoniacal silver nitrate, [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, warmed with an aldehyde → **silver mirror**: RCHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 3OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + 2Ag + 2H₂O + 4NH₃.
- **Fehling's test**: Fehling A (CuSO₄) + Fehling B (alkaline sodium potassium tartrate) warmed with an aliphatic aldehyde → **reddish-brown Cu₂O** precipitate. Aromatic aldehydes do not respond.
- **Haloform reaction**: compounds with CH₃CO– (methyl ketones, ethanal) + NaOX (X₂/NaOH) → haloform CHX₃ + carboxylate. With iodine: yellow **iodoform** — the **iodoform test** (also given by alcohols with CH₃CH(OH)– since they are oxidised to methyl ketones). C=C double bond, if present, is not attacked.

**Reactions due to α-hydrogen** — α-H is acidic because of the electron-withdrawing C=O and the resonance-stabilised **enolate** anion.
- **Aldol condensation**: aldehydes/ketones with at least one α-H, in dilute alkali → β-hydroxy aldehyde (**aldol**) or β-hydroxy ketone (**ketol**), which easily lose water on heating to α,β-unsaturated carbonyls. 2CH₃CHO → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO → but-2-enal.
- **Cross aldol**: between two different carbonyl compounds — gives a mixture of four products if both have α-H; with one partner lacking α-H (benzaldehyde) it is useful, e.g. benzaldehyde + acetophenone → benzalacetophenone (chalcone).

**Other reactions**
- **Cannizzaro reaction**: aldehydes **without α-H** (HCHO, C₆H₅CHO) with concentrated alkali undergo self oxidation-reduction (disproportionation): 2HCHO + conc. KOH → CH₃OH + HCOOK.
- **Electrophilic substitution** in aromatic aldehydes/ketones: –CHO, –COR are **meta-directing and deactivating** (benzaldehyde + HNO₃/H₂SO₄ → m-nitrobenzaldehyde).

check.q: Which gives a positive iodoform test?
check.why: Propanone has a CH₃CO– group, which is trihalogenated and cleaved to yellow CHI₃.

sections.md:
- Methanal (formalin, 40%) preserves biological specimens; makes bakelite (phenol–formaldehyde resin), urea–formaldehyde glues and other polymers.
- Ethanal is a starting material for ethanoic acid, ethyl acetate, vinyl acetate, polymers and drugs.
- Benzaldehyde is used in perfumery and dye industries.
- Acetone and ethyl methyl ketone are common industrial solvents.
- Many are flavour and fragrance compounds: butyraldehyde, vanillin, acetophenone, camphor.

check.q: Formalin is a 40% aqueous solution of
check.why: Formalin is about 40% methanal (formaldehyde) in water, used to preserve specimens.

sections.md:
**Nomenclature**: common names reflect natural sources — formic acid (Latin *formica*, ant), acetic (*acetum*, vinegar), butyric (*butyrum*, butter). IUPAC: -e → **-oic acid** (methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic); for –COOH on a ring: *carboxylic acid* (cyclohexanecarboxylic acid); benzoic acid; HOOC–COOH ethanedioic acid (oxalic); HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH hexanedioic acid (adipic); phthalic acid = benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid.

**Structure**: the carboxyl carbon is sp², planar; the group is less electrophilic than in aldehydes/ketones because of resonance with the –OH oxygen.

**Preparation**
1. **From 1° alcohols and aldehydes**: KMnO₄ (neutral/acid/alkaline) or K₂Cr₂O₇/CrO₃ in acid.
2. **From alkylbenzenes**: vigorous oxidation (chromic acid, acidic or alkaline KMnO₄) oxidises the whole side chain to –COOH regardless of length — all give benzoic acid (needs at least one benzylic H). Alkenes are cleaved too.
3. **From nitriles and amides**: hydrolysis with H⁺ or OH⁻ (mild conditions stop at amide).
4. **From Grignard reagents**: RMgX + CO₂ (dry ice) → salt of carboxylic acid → H₃O⁺ → RCOOH (adds one carbon).
5. **From acyl halides and anhydrides**: hydrolysis with water gives acids; with aqueous base gives carboxylate ions.
6. **From esters**: acidic hydrolysis → acid; basic hydrolysis (saponification) → carboxylate, then acidify.

check.q: Oxidation of propylbenzene with hot KMnO₄ gives
check.why: The whole alkyl side chain is oxidised to a single –COOH group on the ring, giving benzoic acid.

sections.h: 9. Physical properties and acidity of carboxylic acids
sections.md:
Aliphatic acids up to nine carbons are colourless liquids with unpleasant odours; higher acids are wax-like solids.

**Boiling points** are higher than aldehydes, ketones and even alcohols of similar mass, because of extensive hydrogen bonding; most exist as **dimers** even in the vapour phase or aprotic solvents.

**Solubility**: C1–C4 acids are miscible with water (hydrogen bonding); solubility falls with chain length. Benzoic acid is nearly insoluble in cold water. They dissolve in benzene, ether, alcohol, chloroform.

**Acidity** — RCOOH ⇌ RCOO⁻ + H⁺. The **carboxylate ion** is stabilised by two equivalent resonance structures (negative charge equally on both oxygens), so carboxylic acids are more acidic than alcohols and phenols (most have pKa 4–5; phenol 10). They react with metals (H₂), alkalis and even **NaHCO₃** (brisk effervescence of CO₂ — a test distinguishing them from phenols, which are too weak to react).

**Effect of substituents**:
- **Electron-withdrawing groups (EWG)** increase acidity by stabilising carboxylate: Cl, F, NO₂, CN. Order: CF₃COOH > CCl₃COOH > CHCl₂COOH > NO₂CH₂COOH > NC–CH₂COOH > FCH₂COOH > ClCH₂COOH > BrCH₂COOH > HCOOH > ClCH₂CH₂COOH > C₆H₅COOH > C₆H₅CH₂COOH > CH₃COOH > CH₃CH₂COOH.
- **Electron-donating groups (EDG)** decrease acidity.
- More halogens → stronger; closer to –COOH → stronger.
- Aromatic: direct attachment of phenyl/vinyl increases acidity versus acetic acid (sp² carbon is more electronegative). In benzoic acids, EWG increase and EDG decrease acidity.

| Acid | pKa |
|---|---|
| CF₃COOH | 0.23 |
| HCOOH | 3.75 |
| C₆H₅COOH | 4.19 |
| CH₃COOH | 4.76 |

check.q: Which test distinguishes benzoic acid from phenol?
check.why: Carboxylic acids are strong enough to release CO₂ from sodium hydrogencarbonate; phenol is not.

sections.h: 10. Reactions of carboxylic acids and uses
sections.md:
**(A) O–H cleavage**: with metals and alkalis → salts (acidity, above).

**(B) C–OH cleavage**
1. **Anhydride formation**: heat with P₂O₅ or conc. H₂SO₄ → acid anhydride (2CH₃COOH → (CH₃CO)₂O).
2. **Esterification**: RCOOH + R′OH (conc. H₂SO₄ or HCl gas) ⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O. Mechanism: protonation of carbonyl oxygen, nucleophilic attack by alcohol, proton transfer, loss of water, deprotonation. Excess alcohol or removal of water drives it forward.
3. **With PCl₅, PCl₃, SOCl₂** → acyl chlorides; SOCl₂ preferred as by-products are gases.
4. **With ammonia** → ammonium salt → heat → amide (CH₃COONH₄ → CH₃CONH₂); phthalic acid gives phthalimide on strong heating.

**(C) Reactions of –COOH group**
1. **Reduction**: LiAlH₄ or diborane → 1° alcohols. Diborane does not reduce esters, nitro or halo groups easily — it is selective.
2. **Decarboxylation**: sodium salts heated with **soda lime** (NaOH + CaO, 3:1) lose CO₂ → alkane with one carbon fewer (CH₃COONa → CH₄). **Kolbe electrolysis** of aqueous sodium/potassium salts gives alkanes with twice the alkyl groups (2CH₃COONa → C₂H₆ at anode).

**(D) Substitution in the hydrocarbon part**
1. **Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction**: acids with α-H + Cl₂ or Br₂ with red phosphorus → **α-halocarboxylic acids** (RCH₂COOH → RCH(X)COOH).
2. **Ring substitution**: –COOH is deactivating and **meta-directing** (benzoic acid + HNO₃/H₂SO₄ → m-nitrobenzoic acid). Benzoic acid does **not** undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions because the deactivating group and AlCl₃ bonding to it block the reaction.

**Uses**: methanoic acid in rubber, textile, dyeing, leather and electroplating; ethanoic acid as solvent and vinegar in food; hexanedioic acid for nylon-6,6; esters of benzoic acid in perfumery; sodium benzoate as food preservative; higher fatty acids for soaps and detergents.

check.q: Sodium ethanoate heated with soda lime gives
check.why: Decarboxylation removes CO₂ and gives an alkane with one carbon fewer — methane.

summary: Aldehydes R–CHO, ketones R–CO–R′, acids R–COOH all contain C=O.
IUPAC endings: -al, -one, -oic acid; carbaldehyde / carboxylic acid for ring attachments.
Carbonyl C is sp², planar and electrophilic; C=O is polar.
Aldehydes: Rosenmund, Stephen, DIBAL-H, Etard, Gatterman–Koch; ketones: dialkylcadmium, nitrile + Grignard, Friedel–Crafts.
B.p.: hydrocarbons < ethers < aldehydes/ketones < alcohols < carboxylic acids.
Nucleophilic addition: aldehydes > ketones (steric and electronic).

sections.md:
Part 1 listed the general methods. Three routes give **ketones specifically**:

1. **From acyl chlorides with dialkylcadmium**: first make R₂Cd from a Grignard reagent: 2RMgX + CdCl₂ → R₂Cd + 2Mg(X)Cl. Then 2R′COCl + R₂Cd → 2R′COR + CdCl₂. Cadmium reagents are less reactive than Grignard reagents, so the reaction stops at the ketone instead of going on to a tertiary alcohol.
2. **From nitriles with Grignard reagents**: CH₃CH₂CN + C₆H₅MgBr (in ether) gives an imine salt, which on acid hydrolysis gives propiophenone, C₆H₅COCH₂CH₃.
3. **From benzene — Friedel–Crafts acylation**: C₆H₆ + RCOCl with anhydrous AlCl₃ → C₆H₅COR + HCl. Acetyl chloride gives acetophenone. Because the acyl group deactivates the ring, there is no over-substitution — a big advantage over Friedel–Crafts alkylation.

**Exam tip:** Rosenmund and Stephen give aldehydes; cadmium, nitrile + Grignard and Friedel–Crafts acylation give ketones. Ozonolysis, alkyne hydration and oxidation of alcohols can give either, depending on the structure.

check.q: Why is R₂Cd used instead of RMgX to make a ketone from an acyl chloride?
options: It is less reactive and stops at the ketone
It is a stronger reducing agent
check.why: A Grignard reagent would attack the ketone formed and give a tertiary alcohol; the milder dialkylcadmium does not.

sections.md:
**Mechanism.** A nucleophile Nu⁻ attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon from a direction roughly perpendicular to the plane of the sp² carbon. The carbon re-hybridises to **sp³**, giving a **tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate**. This intermediate then picks up a proton (H⁺) from the medium to give the neutral addition product.

**Why aldehydes react faster than ketones**
- *Steric*: an aldehyde carbon carries one H and one group; a ketone carbon carries two bulky groups that block the nucleophile.
- *Electronic*: alkyl groups push electrons (+I effect) into the carbonyl carbon, reducing its positive character. Two alkyl groups in ketones do this more.
- Order: HCHO > CH₃CHO > CH₃COCH₃. **Benzaldehyde is less reactive than propanal** because resonance with the ring makes the carbonyl carbon less electron-poor.

**The key additions**
| Reagent | Product | Note |
|---|---|---|
| HCN (base catalysed, CN⁻) | cyanohydrin | adds one carbon; useful synthetic step |
| NaHSO₃ | bisulphite addition compound (crystalline) | used to separate/purify aldehydes; reversed by dilute acid or alkali |
| Grignard RMgX then H₃O⁺ | alcohols | HCHO → 1°, other aldehydes → 2°, ketones → 3° |
| Alcohols, dry HCl | hemiacetal → acetal (aldehyde); ketone + ethylene glycol → ethylene glycol ketal | acetals protect the carbonyl group; dilute acid regenerates it |
| NH₃ derivatives H₂N–Z (acid catalysed, pH ≈ 3.5) | C=N–Z + H₂O | addition followed by elimination |

**Ammonia derivatives** (Z group → product): –OH → oxime; –NH₂ → hydrazone; –NHC₆H₅ → phenylhydrazone; –NH–C₆H₃(NO₂)₂ → 2,4-DNP derivative (orange-red solid, a classic test); –NHCONH₂ → semicarbazone. Weakly acidic conditions are needed: too much acid protonates the nitrogen nucleophile, too little fails to activate the carbonyl.

check.q: Which is most reactive towards nucleophilic addition?
check.why: Ethanal is an aliphatic aldehyde with only one small alkyl group, so it has the least steric hindrance and no resonance stabilisation of the carbonyl.

sections.md:
- **Clemmensen reduction**: C=O → CH₂ with zinc amalgam + conc. HCl.
- **Wolff–Kishner reduction**: C=O → CH₂ via hydrazone, heated with KOH in ethylene glycol.
- **Tollens' test**: aldehyde + ammoniacal AgNO₃ → bright **silver mirror**; RCHO → RCOO⁻.
- **Fehling's test**: aliphatic aldehyde + Fehling's A (CuSO₄) & B (sodium potassium tartrate, alkaline) → **red-brown Cu₂O**. Aromatic aldehydes do not respond.
- **Haloform reaction**: methyl ketones (and CH₃CHO, CH₃CH(OH)– alcohols) + NaOX → haloform CHX₃ + carboxylate; with I₂/NaOH gives yellow **iodoform**, CHI₃. C=C double bonds, if any, are not attacked.
- **Aldol condensation**: aldehydes/ketones with at least one **α-H**, dilute NaOH → β-hydroxy aldehyde (aldol) or β-hydroxy ketone (ketol), which loses water on heating to give an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl. 2CH₃CHO → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO → CH₃CH=CHCHO (but-2-enal).
- **Cross aldol**: two different carbonyls → a mixture of four products; with one partner lacking α-H (e.g. benzaldehyde + acetophenone) a single main product forms (Claisen–Schmidt).
- **Cannizzaro reaction**: aldehydes **without α-H** (HCHO, C₆H₅CHO) + conc. alkali → disproportionate into an alcohol and a carboxylate salt. 2HCHO + conc. KOH → CH₃OH + HCOOK.
- **Electrophilic substitution** in aromatic carbonyls: –CHO and –COR are deactivating, **meta-directing** groups (benzaldehyde + HNO₃/H₂SO₄ → m-nitrobenzaldehyde).
- **HVZ reaction** (acids): RCH₂COOH + X₂ with red P → α-halo acid.
- **Kolbe electrolysis**: aqueous sodium/potassium carboxylate electrolysed → alkane (2RCOO⁻ → R–R + 2CO₂).
- **Decarboxylation**: sodium carboxylate + soda lime (NaOH + CaO), heat → alkane with one carbon fewer.

check.q: Which aldehyde undergoes Cannizzaro reaction?
check.why: Cannizzaro needs an aldehyde with no α-hydrogen; benzaldehyde's CHO is attached directly to the ring.

sections.md:
Examiners love 'give one chemical test to distinguish'. Learn the logic, not just the list.

| Pair | Test | Positive result |
|---|---|---|
| Propanal vs propanone | Tollens' or Fehling's | propanal gives silver mirror / red ppt |
| Acetophenone vs benzophenone | Iodoform (I₂/NaOH) | acetophenone (a methyl ketone) gives yellow CHI₃ |
| Benzaldehyde vs acetophenone | Tollens' | benzaldehyde gives silver mirror |
| Ethanal vs methanal | Iodoform | ethanal gives yellow ppt |
| Pentan-2-one vs pentan-3-one | Iodoform | pentan-2-one positive |
| Benzoic acid vs phenol | NaHCO₃ | benzoic acid gives brisk CO₂ effervescence |
| Benzaldehyde vs ethanal | Fehling's | ethanal gives red ppt (aromatic aldehydes do not) |
| Ethanoic acid vs ethanal | NaHCO₃ | acid effervesces |

**Why NaHCO₃ separates acids from phenols:** carboxylic acids (pKa ≈ 4–5) are stronger than carbonic acid; phenol (pKa ≈ 10) is weaker, so it cannot release CO₂.

check.q: Which reagent distinguishes pentan-2-one from pentan-3-one?
check.why: Only pentan-2-one has a CH₃CO– group, so only it gives yellow iodoform.

sections.h: 15. Acidity in depth and acid derivatives
sections.md:
A carboxylate ion is stabilised by **two equivalent resonance structures** — the negative charge is shared equally by two oxygens. In phenoxide the charge spreads onto less electronegative carbons, so phenol is a much weaker acid.

**Substituent effects**
- **Electron-withdrawing groups** (–NO₂, –CN, –F, –Cl, –CF₃) stabilise the anion → stronger acid. More such groups and closer to –COOH → stronger.
- **Electron-donating groups** (alkyl) destabilise the anion → weaker acid.
- Order examples: CF₃COOH > CCl₃COOH > CHCl₂COOH > ClCH₂COOH > HCOOH > C₆H₅COOH > CH₃COOH. FCH₂COOH > ClCH₂COOH > BrCH₂COOH (electronegativity). 2-chlorobutanoic > 3-chlorobutanoic > 4-chlorobutanoic acid (distance).
- Directly attaching phenyl or vinyl increases acidity compared with ethanoic acid (sp² carbon is more electronegative).

**Reactions involving the –OH group** produce derivatives: with PCl₅, PCl₃ or SOCl₂ → acyl chloride (SOCl₂ preferred — by-products SO₂ and HCl are gases); with alcohol + conc. H₂SO₄ → ester (esterification, reversible); heating with P₂O₅ or with conc. H₂SO₄ → anhydride; with NH₃ → ammonium salt → amide on heating. **Reduction**: LiAlH₄ or diborane reduces –COOH to –CH₂OH (diborane leaves esters, nitro and halo groups alone).

**Ring substitution**: –COOH is deactivating and meta-directing; benzoic acid does not undergo Friedel–Crafts reactions because the AlCl₃ binds to the carboxyl group.

check.q: Which is the strongest acid?
check.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative substituent, so its –I effect stabilises the carboxylate ion most.

sections.md:
Most conversion questions combine two or three steps from this chapter.

- **Ethanol → 3-hydroxybutanal**: oxidise ethanol (PCC) → ethanal; dil. NaOH → aldol.
- **Benzaldehyde → benzophenone**: KMnO₄ oxidation → benzoic acid; with Ca(OH)₂ → calcium benzoate; dry distillation of calcium benzoate gives benzophenone (or: acid → acyl chloride, then Friedel–Crafts with benzene).
- **Propanone → propene**: NaBH₄ → propan-2-ol; conc. H₂SO₄, heat → propene.
- **Benzoic acid → benzaldehyde**: SOCl₂ → benzoyl chloride; H₂, Pd–BaSO₄ (Rosenmund).
- **Ethanoic acid → methanamine**: NH₃, heat → ethanamide; Br₂/NaOH (Hoffmann bromamide) → CH₃NH₂.
- **Toluene → benzoic acid**: alkaline KMnO₄, then acidify.
- **Bromobenzene → benzoic acid**: Mg/ether → PhMgBr; dry ice (CO₂) then H₃O⁺.
- **Butan-1-ol → butanoic acid**: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ or KMnO₄.

**Did you know?** Synthetic chemists 'protect' an aldehyde as an acetal before attacking another part of a molecule with a Grignard reagent, then remove the acetal with dilute acid — like putting a cap on a pen before shaking the bag.

check.why: Rosenmund reduction uses poisoned palladium so the reduction stops at the aldehyde.

rd-school-c12-economics-a.government-bud.title: Government Budget and the Economy
rd-school-c12-economics-a.government-bud.subtitle: Every February 1st the Finance Minister opens a briefcase — here is what is inside and why it moves the economy

sections.h: 1. Why the government is part of the economy
sections.md:
On 1 February each year, the Union Finance Minister presents the Budget in Parliament. Within minutes, TV tickers flash: *income-tax slabs changed, railway capex raised, fiscal deficit target 4.4% of GDP*. Why does a single speech matter to a cricket-bat maker in Meerut, a farmer in Punjab or a student in Kochi?

Because in a **mixed economy** like India, the government is a giant economic agent. It collects taxes, spends on roads, schools, defence and subsidies, borrows, and lends. Some goods markets cannot supply well at all — **public goods**.

**Public goods vs private goods.** A private good (a samosa, a bike) is **rivalrous** — if I eat it, you cannot — and **excludable** — the seller can keep out those who do not pay. A public good (national defence, street lighting, a public park, flood control) is **non-rivalrous** (my use does not reduce yours) and **non-excludable** (it is hard to stop non-payers). This creates the **free-rider problem**: people enjoy benefits without paying, so private firms will not supply enough. The government therefore provides them, paid for by taxes.

Note: *public provision* is not the same as *public production*. The government may provide a road but hire a private contractor to build it.

The **Constitution of India (Article 112)** requires the government to place before Parliament an **'Annual Financial Statement'** — the Budget — for each financial year (1 April to 31 March).

check.q: Which feature makes national defence a public good?
options: It is produced by the army
It is sold at a low price
check.why: One citizen's protection does not reduce another's, and nobody in the country can be excluded from it, so markets underprovide it.

sections.md:
Following the economist Richard Musgrave, the budget performs three functions:

**1. Allocation function** — providing public goods and deciding the mix of goods in the economy. Through spending (on defence, roads, research) and through taxes and subsidies, the government steers resources into areas the market neglects, and away from harmful ones (high taxes on tobacco).

**2. Redistribution function** — reducing inequality of income and wealth. **Progressive taxation** (higher rates on higher incomes) plus **transfer payments** (old-age pensions, scholarships, free food grains under PMGKAY, MGNREGA wages) change the distribution of **personal disposable income**. Disposable income = factor income – taxes + transfers.

**3. Stabilisation function** — reducing fluctuations in output, employment and prices. Private spending can be too low (recession, unemployment) or too high (inflation). The government raises spending or cuts taxes in a slump and does the opposite in a boom.

Other objectives often listed: **economic growth** (capital expenditure on infrastructure), **managing public enterprises**, and **reducing regional disparities**.

check.q: Higher income-tax rates on the rich combined with pensions for the elderly poor serve the
check.why: Taxing high incomes and transferring to low incomes changes the distribution of disposable income.

sections.md:
The budget has two parts: the **revenue budget** and the **capital budget**.

**Revenue receipts** are receipts that **neither create a liability nor reduce assets** of the government. They are *non-redeemable* — the government never pays them back.

**(a) Tax revenue**
- **Direct taxes**: borne by the person on whom they are imposed and cannot be shifted — personal income tax, corporation tax (on company profits). Earlier also wealth tax, gift tax, estate duty (now abolished).
- **Indirect taxes**: imposed on goods and services, can be shifted to buyers — **Goods and Services Tax (GST)**, customs duties (on imports/exports), excise duties (on petroleum products, liquor, now largely subsumed by GST).

**(b) Non-tax revenue**
- Interest receipts on loans given by the Centre (to states, public enterprises).
- Dividends and profits from public sector undertakings (and the RBI surplus transfer).
- Fees (passport, court fees), licences, fines and penalties.
- External grants-in-aid.
- Revenue from government services (e.g. railways' contribution, broadcasting).

> **Box — GST (introduced 1 July 2017)**: 'One Nation, One Tax'. GST replaced a maze of central and state indirect taxes (central excise, service tax, VAT, entry tax etc.) with a single destination-based tax on goods and services. A GST Council of the Union Finance Minister and state finance ministers sets rates (multiple slabs). It aims at a common national market, fewer cascading taxes (tax on tax) and easier compliance, with input tax credit for businesses.

sections.md:
**Revenue expenditure** is spending that **neither creates physical/financial assets nor reduces liabilities** — the day-to-day running cost of government: salaries, pensions, **interest payments** on past debt, **subsidies** (food, fertiliser, LPG), defence services, grants to states (even if states use them to build assets, for the Centre they are revenue spending).

It is split into expenditure on general services (interest, administration, defence), economic services (agriculture, industry, power, transport) and social services (education, health) — and grants to states. **Interest payments** are among the largest items of revenue expenditure in recent budgets.

**Capital receipts** either **create a liability** or **reduce financial assets**:
- **Borrowings** from the public (market loans, treasury bills), from the RBI and from abroad — create liabilities.
- **Recovery of loans** given earlier to states and PSUs — reduces assets.
- **Disinvestment** — selling the government's shares in PSUs (e.g. Air India's sale) — reduces assets.
- Small savings (Post Office deposits, PPF) and provident funds.

**Capital expenditure** either **creates assets** or **reduces liabilities**:
- Buying land, buildings, machinery; building roads, railways, ports, dams.
- Investment in shares; loans and advances to states, PSUs and others.
- **Repayment of loans**.

Another classification: **plan and non-plan** expenditure was used until 2016–17; it was dropped from 2017–18 when the Planning Commission ended. Budget documents now focus on revenue vs capital.

| | Creates liability / reduces asset? | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue receipt | No | Income tax, dividends |
| Capital receipt | Yes | Borrowing, disinvestment |
| Revenue expenditure | No asset created | Salaries, interest, subsidies |
| Capital expenditure | Creates asset / cuts liability | Highway, loan repayment |

check.q: Repayment of a loan by the government is
check.why: Repaying a loan reduces the government's liabilities, which is the test for capital expenditure.

sections.h: 5. Balanced, surplus and deficit budgets; measures of deficit
sections.md:
If estimated receipts equal estimated expenditure, the budget is **balanced**; receipts > expenditure is a **surplus**; expenditure > receipts is a **deficit budget**. Most modern budgets — including India's — are deficit budgets. The deficit is always met by borrowing (a capital receipt), so in the accounting sense receipts and payments still balance; what matters is the *composition*.

**1. Revenue deficit** = Revenue expenditure – Revenue receipts.
It shows the government is **dissaving** — borrowing to pay for consumption (salaries, interest), not assets. This reduces future capacity: borrowed money must be repaid with interest, while no asset earns a return. A high revenue deficit is a warning sign.

**2. Fiscal deficit** = Total expenditure – (Revenue receipts + non-debt-creating capital receipts).
Non-debt capital receipts = recovery of loans + disinvestment proceeds (+ other receipts that do not add to debt). Therefore **fiscal deficit = total borrowing requirement** of the government from all sources.
- From the financing side: fiscal deficit = net borrowing at home + borrowing from RBI + borrowing from abroad.
- A rising fiscal deficit adds to **public debt**, and interest on the debt adds to future revenue expenditure — a vicious circle that can lead to a **debt trap**.
- **Gross fiscal deficit** includes the revenue deficit; the share of fiscal deficit used to cover revenue deficit tells us how much borrowing finances consumption.

**3. Primary deficit** = Fiscal deficit – Interest payments.
It strips away the burden of *past* borrowing and shows how much the government is borrowing for its *current* needs. A zero primary deficit means borrowing is only for paying interest.

sections.h: 6. Fiscal policy in the Keynesian model
sections.md:
**Fiscal policy** = the government's use of spending and taxation to influence aggregate demand and hence output and employment. (Read alongside the chapter on income determination.)

With government, aggregate demand AD = C + I + G, where consumption C = C̄ + c(Y – T + TR), c is the marginal propensity to consume (MPC), T taxes and TR transfers.

Equilibrium: Y = C̄ + c(Y – T + TR) + I + G, which solves to

Y* = [C̄ – cT + cTR + I + G] / (1 – c)

**Government expenditure multiplier**: ΔY/ΔG = **1/(1 – c)**. With c = 0.8, a ₹100 crore rise in G raises output by ₹500 crore.

**Tax multiplier** (lump-sum tax): ΔY/ΔT = **–c/(1 – c)**. With c = 0.8: –4. A ₹100 crore tax cut raises output by ₹400 crore — smaller than the G multiplier because part of the tax cut is saved, while G is spent directly.

**Transfer multiplier**: ΔY/ΔTR = **c/(1 – c)** — same size as the tax multiplier, opposite sign.

**Balanced budget multiplier**: if G and T rise by the same amount, ΔY = ΔG × [1/(1–c) – c/(1–c)] = ΔG × 1. So the **balanced budget multiplier = 1**: equal increases in spending and taxes raise output by exactly that amount.

**Proportional taxes**: if T = tY, the multiplier becomes **1/[1 – c(1 – t)]**, smaller than 1/(1 – c). Proportional income taxes act as **automatic stabilisers**: when income falls, tax collections fall automatically and soften the drop in disposable income; transfers like unemployment benefits do the same. They operate without new decisions — 'built-in stability'.

**Expansionary fiscal policy** (↑G, ↓T) fights a deflationary gap; **contractionary policy** (↓G, ↑T) fights inflation. Discretionary policy needs deliberate decisions; automatic stabilisers work on their own.

sections.md:
**Is a deficit harmful?** Arguments on both sides:
- **Burden on future generations**: today's borrowing must be repaid, through higher taxes on future citizens. Economist David Ricardo noted that rational households may save more in anticipation of future taxes (**Ricardian equivalence**), weakening the effect of deficits.
- **Crowding out**: when the government borrows heavily, interest rates may rise and private investment falls. But if the economy has unemployed resources, government spending can raise income, savings and even investment (crowding in).
- **What the deficit buys matters**: borrowing for productive capital (roads, ports, power) can raise growth and future revenue; borrowing for consumption does not.
- **Inflation**: financing deficits by printing money (borrowing from the central bank, *monetisation*) can cause inflation if the economy is near full capacity. India ended automatic monetisation through ad hoc treasury bills by an agreement with the RBI in 1997.
- **Ways to reduce the deficit**: raise tax revenue (wider base, better compliance), sell PSU shares, cut wasteful expenditure, rationalise subsidies — and grow the economy so revenue rises.

**Public debt** is the accumulated sum of past borrowings. Debt is sustainable if the **debt-to-GDP ratio** stays stable; this depends on whether GDP grows faster than the interest rate on debt.

> **Box — FRBM Act, 2003**: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act set targets to eliminate the revenue deficit and bring the fiscal deficit to 3% of GDP, required the government to present fiscal policy statements with the budget (Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement, Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement, Macroeconomic Framework Statement), and limited borrowing from the RBI. Targets have been revised several times — e.g. relaxed during the 2008 global crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic (2020–21), when India's fiscal deficit rose sharply to support the economy — and the government has since followed a glide path to bring it down.

sections.h: 8. Taxes up close: direct, indirect, progressive
sections.md:
Every February the Finance Minister reads out tax changes and the whole country listens — salaried people for income-tax slabs, shopkeepers for GST rates. Let us sort taxes properly.

**Direct taxes** fall on the person who pays them and cannot be shifted: personal income tax, corporation tax. **Indirect taxes** are paid to the government by one person but their burden can be passed on to others through prices: GST, customs duty, excise on petrol.

**By the way they change with income**
- **Progressive**: the rate rises as income rises (India's income-tax slabs). Rich people pay a larger *share* of income, which reduces inequality — an aim of the budget's *redistribution* function.
- **Proportional**: the same rate for all income levels (a flat tax).
- **Regressive**: the share of income paid falls as income rises. A uniform tax on salt is regressive in effect, because the poor spend a larger part of income on it.

**Did you know?** GST (Goods and Services Tax), introduced in India on 1 July 2017, replaced many central and state indirect taxes with one tax collected at each stage on value added. It is shared between the Centre and the states.

**Non-tax revenue** is also part of revenue receipts: interest on loans given by the government, dividends and profits of public sector enterprises, fees, fines, licence charges and grants from foreign governments.

check.q: A tax whose rate rises with income is called
check.why: Under a progressive tax both the amount and the share of income paid rise as income rises.

sections.md:
Capital receipts either **create a liability** or **reduce assets** of the government.

- **Borrowings** — from the public (market loans, bonds), from the RBI, from abroad. These create a liability: they must be repaid with interest.
- **Recovery of loans** given earlier to states or PSUs — reduces an asset (the loan).
- **Disinvestment** — selling the government's shares in public sector enterprises. It reduces assets. Economists warn that using disinvestment to cover current spending is like selling the family jewellery to pay the grocery bill.
- Small savings (Post Office deposits, PPF) are also borrowings.

**Quick test**: ask two questions. Does it create a liability? Does it reduce an asset? If either answer is yes, it is a capital receipt. Income tax: no and no → revenue receipt. Loan from the World Bank: liability → capital receipt. Sale of shares of a PSU: asset reduced → capital receipt.

check.q: Disinvestment is a capital receipt because it
check.why: Selling the government's shareholding reduces the assets it owns.

sections.md:
Three measures, each answering a different question:

- **Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts.** Is the government borrowing to pay for day-to-day consumption?
- **Fiscal deficit = Total expenditure − (Revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts).** How much must the government borrow this year? Non-debt capital receipts = recovery of loans + disinvestment.
- **Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Interest payments.** How much borrowing is for *current* needs, leaving out the burden of past loans?

**Example (₹ crore)**: Revenue receipts 20,000; revenue expenditure 26,000 of which interest 4,000; capital expenditure 9,000; recoveries of loans 500; disinvestment 1,500.
- Revenue deficit = 26,000 − 20,000 = **6,000**
- Total expenditure = 26,000 + 9,000 = 35,000; non-debt receipts = 20,000 + 500 + 1,500 = 22,000
- Fiscal deficit = 35,000 − 22,000 = **13,000** (this equals the borrowing needed)
- Primary deficit = 13,000 − 4,000 = **9,000**

A high revenue deficit is the most worrying: it means borrowed money is spent on consumption, which builds no asset to repay the loan from.

**How a deficit is financed**: borrowing from the public (raises interest rates, may *crowd out* private investment) or borrowing from the RBI (deficit financing / printing money — can be inflationary).

check.q: If fiscal deficit is ₹50,000 crore and interest payments are ₹18,000 crore, the primary deficit is
check.why: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest = 50,000 − 18,000 = 32,000.

sections.h: 11. The three multipliers of fiscal policy
sections.md:
Extend the Keynesian model: Y = C + I + G, with C = C̄ + c(Y − T). Solving gives

Y = (C̄ − cT + I + G) / (1 − c)

- **Government expenditure multiplier**: ΔY/ΔG = 1/(1 − c). With c = 0.8 it is 5: an extra ₹100 crore spent on roads raises income by ₹500 crore.
- **Tax multiplier**: ΔY/ΔT = −c/(1 − c). With c = 0.8 it is −4. A tax cut works *more weakly* than spending, because part of the extra disposable income is saved before it is spent.
- **Transfers** (pensions, subsidies paid in cash) work like negative taxes: multiplier +c/(1 − c).
- **Balanced-budget multiplier**: raise G and T by the same amount. ΔY = ΔG/(1 − c) − cΔG/(1 − c) = ΔG. The multiplier is **1** — income rises by exactly the rise in spending.

**Proportional taxes** (T = tY) reduce the multiplier to 1/(1 − c(1 − t)). With c = 0.8 and t = 0.25: 1/(1 − 0.6) = 2.5. Such taxes act as **automatic stabilisers**: in a boom tax collections rise automatically and slow spending; in a slump they fall and cushion incomes, without any new decision by Parliament.

sections.md:
Each year's fiscal deficit adds to the **stock of public debt**. Is that a problem?

**Arguments that debt is a burden**
- Future generations must pay taxes to cover interest and repayment.
- Large borrowing can push up interest rates and **crowd out** private investment.
- If interest payments grow faster than revenue, the government borrows just to pay interest — a debt trap.
- Borrowing from the central bank can create inflation.

**Arguments that it need not be**
- If borrowing builds productive assets (railways, power, schools), the higher future output can repay the loan.
- Internal debt is owed by citizens to citizens; it redistributes rather than simply destroys wealth.
- *Ricardian equivalence* (a view some economists hold): forward-looking people save more today to pay expected future taxes, so a deficit may not raise demand at all. Others doubt that people behave this way.

**India's rules**: the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003, set targets to reduce fiscal and revenue deficits and made the government present medium-term fiscal plans. Targets have been revised several times, and there was large borrowing during the pandemic (2020–21).

A useful measure is the **debt–GDP ratio**: debt can grow and still be sustainable if GDP grows faster.

options: government spending replaces private investment through higher interest rates
check.why: Heavy government borrowing raises interest rates, which discourages private firms from investing.

rd-school-c12-economics-a.income-determi.title: Determination of Income and Employment
rd-school-c12-economics-a.income-determi.subtitle: Why one extra rupee spent on a highway can become five rupees of national income

sections.h: 1. The big question: what decides total output?
sections.md:
In 2020 lockdowns, factories in Tiruppur fell silent and lakhs of migrant workers lost jobs — not because machines broke or skills vanished, but because people *stopped buying*. This chapter builds the simplest model of how **aggregate demand** determines a country's income and employment in the short run.

The ideas come from **John Maynard Keynes** (*The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money*, 1936), written during the Great Depression. Classical economists believed markets automatically bring full employment; Keynes argued that an economy could get stuck with unemployed workers and idle machines because demand was too low.

**Key assumptions of the simple model:**
- Short run; the **price level is fixed** (firms supply whatever is demanded at the given price — supply is perfectly elastic).
- **Rate of interest is fixed**; investment is decided independently (*autonomous*).
- At first, a **two-sector economy** (households and firms) with no government and no foreign trade.
- 'Income', 'output' and 'GDP' are used interchangeably.

We will cover, in NCERT order: aggregate demand and its components (consumption, investment), ex ante vs ex post, determination of income in the short run (algebraic and graphical), effect of autonomous changes, the **multiplier**, and the problems of **excess and deficient demand** (and the paradox of thrift).

check.q: In the simple Keynesian model, the price level is assumed to be
check.why: Keynes's short-run analysis takes prices as fixed so output adjusts to demand.

sections.h: 2. Ex ante and ex post; consumption
sections.md:
**Ex ante** means *planned* or *intended* (what people wish to do). **Ex post** means *actual* or *realised* (what actually happened, as recorded in accounts). National income accounting deals with ex post values; income determination deals with ex ante plans. Planned investment may differ from actual investment because of **unplanned changes in inventories**.

**Consumption function.** Households' planned consumption depends on income:

C = C̄ + cY

- **C̄** = **autonomous consumption** — spending even at zero income (from past savings or borrowing) for basic needs.
- **c** = **marginal propensity to consume (MPC)** = ΔC/ΔY, the share of an extra rupee of income that is consumed; 0 ≤ c ≤ 1.
- **cY** = **induced consumption** (depends on income).

**Saving** S = Y – C = –C̄ + (1 – c)Y. **MPS** = ΔS/ΔY = s = 1 – c, so **MPC + MPS = 1**.

**Average propensities**: APC = C/Y, APS = S/Y, and APC + APS = 1. APC can exceed 1 at low income (dissaving), and it falls as income rises; APS can be negative.

| Y | C (= 40 + 0.8Y) | S | APC | APS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 40 | –40 | — | — |
| 100 | 120 | –20 | 1.2 | –0.2 |
| 200 | 200 | 0 | 1.0 | 0 |
| 300 | 280 | 20 | 0.93 | 0.07 |
| 400 | 360 | 40 | 0.9 | 0.1 |

The income at which C = Y (here 200) is the **break-even point**; saving is zero.

sections.md:
**Investment** = addition to the stock of physical capital (machines, buildings, roads) plus changes in inventories. In the simple model, planned investment is **autonomous**: I = Ī — decided by firms' expectations, interest rates and business confidence, not by current income.

**Aggregate demand (AD)** in a two-sector economy = planned consumption + planned investment:

AD = C + I = C̄ + Ī + cY = **Ā + cY**, where Ā = C̄ + Ī is **autonomous expenditure**.

AD is a straight line with intercept Ā and slope c (< 1), so it is flatter than the 45° line.

In an open economy with government, AD = C + I + G + (X – M), but we keep G and net exports autonomous and initially zero for simplicity.

**Aggregate supply** in this model: since prices are fixed and firms produce what is demanded, the AS curve is drawn as the **45° line**, on which every point satisfies AD = Y — total expenditure equals output.

check.q: The slope of the aggregate demand line in the simple model is
check.why: AD = Ā + cY, so each extra rupee of income adds c rupees of planned spending.

sections.h: 4. Determination of equilibrium income in the short run
sections.md:
**Equilibrium** occurs where **planned aggregate demand = output**:

Y = AD = Ā + cY → **Y* = Ā/(1 – c)**

**Graphically**: the point where the AD line cuts the 45° line.

**Why it is stable (inventory adjustment):**
- If output Y₁ > Y* — AD < output → unsold goods pile up, **unplanned inventories rise** → firms cut output.
- If output Y₂ < Y* — AD > output → inventories fall **below planned levels** → firms raise output.

Only at Y* do firms find that sales match production.

**Equivalent saving–investment approach**: since Y = C + S and AD = C + I, the condition Y = AD gives **S = I** (ex ante, planned saving = planned investment). On a graph, the saving function S = –C̄ + (1 – c)Y cuts the horizontal investment line I = Ī at Y*.

Remember: **ex post** (actual) saving always equals actual investment, because unplanned inventory change is counted in actual investment. Only planned values can differ.

**Effect of an autonomous change**: if Ī rises, the AD line shifts up parallel and equilibrium moves right. If c rises, the AD line becomes steeper, also raising Y*.

sections.md:
Suppose a company spends ₹100 crore building a factory in Sanand. That ₹100 crore becomes income for cement suppliers, workers and engineers. With MPC = 0.8 they spend ₹80 crore on food, clothes and phones — which becomes income for shopkeepers and farmers, who spend ₹64 crore, and so on.

Total rise in income = 100 + 80 + 64 + 51.2 + … = 100 × (1 + 0.8 + 0.8² + …) = 100 × 1/(1 – 0.8) = **₹500 crore**.

**Multiplier** k = ΔY/ΔĀ = **1/(1 – c) = 1/MPS**.

| MPC | MPS | Multiplier |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 0.5 | 2 |
| 0.75 | 0.25 | 4 |
| 0.8 | 0.2 | 5 |
| 0.9 | 0.1 | 10 |

**Points to note:**
- The higher the MPC, the larger the multiplier.
- Minimum value is 1 (MPC = 0); it would be infinite if MPC = 1.
- The process works in reverse: a fall in investment lowers income by a multiple.
- **Rounds**: the multiplier acts through successive rounds of spending; each round is smaller by the factor c.
- It applies to any autonomous change — investment, autonomous consumption, government spending, exports.
- It needs spare capacity (unemployed resources); at full employment, extra demand raises prices instead (outside this model).

**Paradox of thrift**: if all households try to save more (MPS rises, or C̄ falls), aggregate demand falls, output falls, and total saving in the end **does not rise** (with autonomous investment, S = I = Ī at the new, lower income) — and may even fall if investment depends on income. What is virtuous for one family can hurt the whole economy in a recession.

sections.h: 6. Full employment, excess and deficient demand
sections.md:
Keynes's crucial point: the equilibrium Y* need not be at **full-employment output (Y_F)** — the output when all who want work at the going wage are employed.

**Deficient demand** (deflationary gap): AD at full-employment output is *less* than Y_F. Equilibrium is below Y_F → **involuntary unemployment**, idle capacity. The gap is the vertical distance between the 45° line and AD at Y_F. Effects: falling output, income and employment; in reality, possibly falling prices.

**Excess demand** (inflationary gap): AD at Y_F *exceeds* Y_F. Output cannot rise beyond full employment, so the excess demand raises **prices** (inflation) without raising real output.

**Measures to correct them:**

| Policy | Deficient demand | Excess demand |
|---|---|---|
| Fiscal | ↑ government spending, ↓ taxes | ↓ spending, ↑ taxes |
| Monetary (RBI) | ↓ repo rate, ↓ CRR/SLR, buy bonds (OMO) | ↑ repo rate, ↑ CRR, sell bonds |
| Credit | easier margins, lower bank rate | higher margin requirements |

The size of the gap needed to correct equals (gap in output)/multiplier: to raise output by ₹1,000 crore with multiplier 4, autonomous spending must rise by ₹250 crore.

> Did you know? During the 2008 global financial crisis and again in 2020, India used expansionary fiscal packages and RBI rate cuts — classic Keynesian tools — to fight deficient demand.

sections.h: 7. Some more concepts: the government and foreign trade in the model
sections.md:
The model extends naturally. Adding government (G, T) gives AD = C̄ + c(Y – T) + Ī + Ḡ; equilibrium Y* = (C̄ – cT + Ī + Ḡ)/(1 – c). The G-multiplier is 1/(1 – c), the lump-sum tax multiplier –c/(1 – c) (studied in detail in the government budget chapter).

In an **open economy**, imports depend on income (M = M̄ + mY, m = marginal propensity to import), and exports are autonomous. Then the multiplier becomes **1/(1 – c + m)** — smaller, because some extra spending leaks abroad. The open-economy chapter develops this.

**Leakages and injections**: saving, taxes and imports are *leakages* from the circular flow; investment, government spending and exports are *injections*. Equilibrium occurs where planned leakages = planned injections: S + T + M = I + G + X.

**Summary of the logic**: output is determined by demand in the short run; an initial change in autonomous spending is magnified by the multiplier; and nothing guarantees that the equilibrium will be at full employment — hence the case for active policy.

rd-school-c12-economics-a.income-determi.title: Determination of Income and Employment (part 2)
rd-school-c12-economics-a.income-determi.subtitle: Propensities, the saving–investment route, the multiplier round by round and the paradox of thrift

sections.md:
Imagine Meena, a schoolteacher in Pune, gets a raise from ₹40,000 to ₹50,000 a month. She now spends ₹42,000 instead of ₹34,000. How do economists describe her behaviour?

- **Average propensity to consume (APC) = C/Y.** Before: 34,000/40,000 = 0.85. After: 42,000/50,000 = 0.84.
- **Marginal propensity to consume (MPC, c) = ΔC/ΔY** = 8,000/10,000 = 0.8.
- **Average propensity to save (APS) = S/Y.** Before: 6,000/40,000 = 0.15.
- **Marginal propensity to save (MPS, s) = ΔS/ΔY** = 2,000/10,000 = 0.2.

Two identities always hold because income is either consumed or saved: **APC + APS = 1** and **MPC + MPS = 1**.

Facts to remember:
- MPC lies between 0 and 1 (people spend part, not all, of extra income).
- APC can be greater than 1 at very low income, because of **autonomous consumption** C̄ — people consume something even at zero income by drawing on past savings or borrowing. At that point saving is negative (*dissaving*).
- With a linear consumption function C = C̄ + cY, APC falls as income rises, while MPC stays constant.
- The income level where C = Y (and S = 0) is the **break-even point**.
